newsitem.title: JAPAN: Oil slicks threatens one of Japan's richest coasts.
newsitem.headline: Oil slicks threatens one of Japan's richest coasts.

text.p: The oil spill from a Russian tanker threatens to ruin one of Japan's richest marine environments for years to come, officials said on Wednesday.
"The immediate effects are hard to measure... I couldn't say if the spills will write off one, two, three or more years of harvests," an official with the Fisheries Disaster Task Force said.

"The seaweed which is covered by the oil is likely to rot and die. In any case, it is completely unfit for human consumption. Birds whose natural habitat is the rocky promontories will also be affected...
"As for deeper ocean dwellers such as crab or fish, it's too early to say... But we expect large damage to the local ecosystem," he said.
The tanker Nakhodka, carrying 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of heavy fuel oil, broke in two and started leaking oil in the Sea of Japan on January 2.
By Wednesday, 100 km (60 miles) of coastline stretching north from Kyoto Prefecture on the Sea of Japan had been fouled by one of the worst oil spills ever to hit Japan.

In 1995, the latest year for which statistics are available, 164,256 tonnes of fish, shellfish, crab, shrimp and squid and other marine produce was caught in the now-threatened area, according to government statistics.
The catch, nearly three percent of national production, was worth a total of 50.6 billion yen ($440 million).
The region is also a leading area for the prized Benizuwai crab, which lives at depths of 400 metres (1,300 feet) and is noted for its succulent white flesh.
Also affected are the "Ama", women traditionally who dive without air tanks or snorkels to harvest seaweed, shellfish and other delicacies.
Their diving methods were chronicled as long ago as the third century.
